# The Space Between Things

I've been thinking about gaps lately. Not the store, though that's funny to imagine—just the actual spaces where nothing happens, where things end and other things begin. These gaps are everywhere once you start noticing them. They're in conversations, in music, in the architecture of days.

My grandmother used to say that the silence between words was just as important as the words themselves. I didn't understand this as a child. I thought silence was a failure, a breakdown in communication. I'd rush to fill it with more words, more noise, more *something*. Now I think she was right about almost everything, which is a peculiar realization to have when someone is no longer here to tell.

There's a gap between falling asleep and being asleep where the most interesting dreams live. You're aware enough to guide them but unaware enough that the rules don't apply. Physics bends. People you loved and lost are suddenly beside you making coffee. Buildings have impossible geometries. In those moments, you're not quite one thing or another, and that's precisely where the magic happens.

I wonder if growth is just gaps—spaces where the old version of you has fallen away but the new version hasn't fully formed yet. We call these the hard times. The in-between. The waiting room of life. But they might be the only times we're actually changing, actually becoming someone different. The rest of the time, we're just settling into who we've already become.

My neighbor has a cat that sits in the exact center of the sidewalk during our walks. It doesn't do anything. It just sits there, perfectly still, watching. I used to think it was broken or ill, but I've realized it's the most present creature I've ever encountered. It's not trying to get anywhere. It's not looking at its phone or thinking about what's for dinner. It's just *sitting*, occupying that small circle of concrete with complete commitment. There's something holy about that.

I've been reading about how mushrooms work, and it turns out that what we see—the fruiting body, the part we eat—is just the reproductive organ of an infinitely larger organism living underground. The real mushroom is this vast network of mycelium spreading through the soil, connecting trees, sharing nutrients, facilitating communication between species. The part we see is almost incidental to what's actually happening. I think people might work similarly. What we show is just the fruiting body. The real architecture of who we are is mostly hidden, mostly in conversation with others.

There's a particular kind of afternoon light that makes me remember being eight years old, though I can't remember what I was actually doing. Just the feeling of it. The golden quality of it. The sense that time was infinite and I had nowhere to be. I wish I could have told that version of me that this feeling would become precious, that one day I'd be hunting for it in old photographs and the exact angle of sunlight on a kitchen wall.

I think we're all secretly convinced that other people have figured out what they're doing, and we're the only one pretending. But what if everyone feels like an impostor? What if that's actually the universal experience, and the people who seem confident are just better at pretending, or have made peace with the pretending? That would mean we're all in it together, all equally confused and doing our best, which is either comforting or terrifying depending on the day.

Language is such a strange thing. We take these arbitrary sounds and scribbles and agree they mean something, and then we build entire civilizations on that agreement. But there's always something that gets lost in translation, even when we're translating between two people speaking the same language. Maybe especially then. I say "I'm tired" and you hear it one way, but I mean it in seven different ways, and you could never fully know which seven.

I've noticed that the older I get, the more I understand my parents, which is its own kind of heartbreaking because it happens too late to make use of that understanding. I see now why my mother was anxious about things. Why my father was so private. Why they made the decisions they made. Understanding arrives like a gift that can't be returned or exchanged, that you can only accept and hold.

There's something about writing that forces you to think more clearly than thinking alone. The thinking alone is foggy, circular, repetitive. But the moment you try to put it into words, you have to commit. You have to take a stance. That's probably why I'm doing this right now, even though I don't know exactly what I'm trying to say. The act of trying to say it is the point.

I've been wondering if nostalgia is just missing the gaps—missing the times when you didn't know how things would turn out. Every happy memory probably had parts that were boring or uncomfortable, but we remember them as golden because we didn't know then what we know now. We can't go back to not knowing, and that's what we're really missing.

Sometimes I think about all the people I've encountered who are now dead. They were real. They had interior lives as complex as mine. Thoughts and dreams and fears. And now they're simply... not. The world continued without them, and that's both obvious and impossible to really grasp.

I think what I'm trying to say, if I'm trying to say anything, is that the gaps are part of it. The not-knowing. The waiting. The silence. The spaces between things are where we actually live. The rest is just what we tell ourselves about the spaces.

But I could be wrong. Tomorrow I might think something completely different, and that's okay too.
